Died in unexplained circumstances at sea Nov 5 1991, buried on the Mount of Olives with state honors. … Media concentration matters because the story travels through the press. Robert Maxwell — British-Czech publisher, documented Mossad connections in Seymour Hersh's The Samson Option [cite:hersh_samson], Tom Bower's biography [cite:bower_maxwell], and Gordon Thomas's subsequent biography — consolidated Mirror Group Newspapers, Macmillan Publishing, Berlitz, and Pergamon Press between 1984 and 1991. He died in unexplained circumstances at sea on 5 November 1991 and received an Israeli state funeral on the Mount of Olives with six intelligence chiefs in attendance. … Born Jan Ludvik Hoch in 1923 in Czechoslovakia, he survived the Holocaust that killed most of his family, served in the British Army, and anglicized his name after the war. By the 1980s he controlled Mirror Group Newspapers — publisher of the Daily Mirror, one of Britain's highest-circulation tabloids — along with the academic publisher Pergamon Press, the textbook and reference giant Macmillan, and the language-education company Berlitz. This was not a fringe operation. Mirror Group alone reached millions of British readers daily. Maxwell's connections to Israeli intelligence are documented in two independent investigative biographies: Gordon Thomas and Martin Dillon's Robert Maxwell, Israel's Superspy (2002), and Tom Bower's earlier Maxwell: The Outsider (1988). - **s16 · Robert Maxwell and the Press Empire (1988–1991)** · Mirror Group (UK press empire): … The pension fund theft was the mechanism by which he sustained apparent liquidity in his final years. [cite:bower_maxwell] The Mirror Group — Robert Maxwell's [1] British press empire, anchored by the Daily Mirror, the Sunday Mirror, the People, and a string of regional papers, one of the two largest tabloid groups in the United Kingdom and a daily presence in millions of working-class British homes. Control of the Mirror gave Maxwell direct command of a mass-circulation megaphone — the power to set headlines, frame stories, and shape the political attention of a huge readership. That is the entity's first significance: whatever else Maxwell was, he was a man who owned the front pages seen by a large share of Britain every morning, which is precisely the kind of concentrated media power the scene's myth of an "independent and objective press" is designed to obscure. The second significance emerged only after his death in November 1991 [5], when investigators discovered that roughly £440 million was missing from the Mirror Group pension funds. Maxwell had been secretly looting the retirement savings of his own employees to prop up the apparent liquidity of his over-leveraged empire in its final years.
